metadata.title: Full-text correction for Ronaghi et al. 2026
metadata.correction: Replaces an abstract-level adjacent bibliographic placeholder with a core, full-text-grounded 52-field extraction and one 12-dimension quality row.

evidence_records.Full citation: Ronaghi, Sasha; Aveling, Emma-Louise; Levis, Maria; Ross, Rachel L.; Alsentzer, Emily; and Singer, Sara, for the iPATH investigators. (2026). Large Language Models for Large-Scale, Rigorous Qualitative Analysis in Applied Health Services Research. arXiv:2601.14478v1. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-7794878/v1
evidence_records.Title: Large Language Models for Large-Scale, Rigorous Qualitative Analysis in Applied Health Services Research
evidence_records.Authors: Sasha Ronaghi; Emma-Louise Aveling; Maria Levis; Rachel L. Ross; Emily Alsentzer; Sara Singer; iPATH investigators
evidence_records.Venue: arXiv:2601.14478v1; related Research Square preprint DOI 10.21203/rs.3.rs-7794878/v1
evidence_records.Publication history notes: arXiv v1 submitted 2026-01-20. The manuscript identifies a related Research Square DOI, 10.21203/rs.3.rs-7794878/v1; a peer-reviewed version was not verified by the review cutoff.
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: iPATH applied-health-services human–LLM qualitative-analysis study; two task-specific workflows on one 12-FQHC comparative-case-study corpus. It cites LLooM/CollabCoder and prior human–LLM coding/theme-comparison studies but reports a distinct applied implementation and evaluation.
evidence_records.Research objective: Propose a model- and task-agnostic framework for designing rigorous task-specific human–LLM qualitative-analysis methods and demonstrate it in two real-world tasks within a multi-site diabetes-care study.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: Comparative case study using qualitative synthesis for actionable cross-site feedback and deductive qualitative coding to refine a practice-transformation intervention; qualitative rigor is evaluated against task-specific grounding, theory/data integration, research-question fit, significance, and practitioner usefulness rather than a single gold standard.
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: Researchers first perform each task manually on a small sample, decompose it into human and model subtasks, compare manual and LLM-assisted outputs at small scale, and then scale the selected workflow. Task 1 organizes researcher-authored site-summary bullets into themes before human synthesis. Task 2 uses researcher-developed subquestions, embedding retrieval, quote-grounded LLM summaries, automated quotation verification/deduplication, LLM relevance sorting, and human contextual interpretation across 167 transcripts.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: hybrid: qualitative synthesis within 22 prespecified care-practice domains plus deductive coding with 19 prespecified practice-area codes
evidence_records.Domain: applied health-services and implementation research; type 2 diabetes care in Federally Qualified Health Centers
evidence_records.Dataset name: Implementing Scalable, PAtient-centered, Team-based, Technology-enabled Care for Adults with Type 2 Diabetes (iPATH) comparative case study
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: restricted; interview data are not public because of sensitivity and confidentiality risk; de-identified excerpts relevant to findings are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request
evidence_records.Number of documents: 167 interview transcripts across 12 FQHCs for Task 2; Task 1 uses researcher-generated site summaries across 12 sites and 22 care-practice domains
evidence_records.Number of participants: not reported; interviewees included clinicians, administrators, patient representatives, and other key stakeholders
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: Task 1: approximately 31,200 words of site summaries. Task 2: approximately 1,327,000 transcript words and 8,600 interview minutes across 167 interviews.
evidence_records.Document length: Per-interview word length not reported; combined transcripts per site averaged 157,179 tokens, and 6 of 12 sites exceeded 128,000 tokens
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: high-risk confidential health-services interview data accessed through Stanford SecureGPT; interview data withheld to protect participant confidentiality
evidence_records.Model family: OpenAI GPT and embedding models; Google Gemini, Anthropic Claude, and DeepSeek were also explored during development
evidence_records.Exact model/version: ChatGPT-4o; OpenAI o1; text-embedding-3-large; Google Gemini 2.5; Claude Sonnet 3.5; DeepSeek r1; dated API snapshots not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: Task 1 asks ChatGPT-4o to preserve and group site-summary bullets into categorical themes with a miscellaneous category, then prompts o1 to synthesize using the task goal, domain definitions, and four manual few-shot examples. Task 2 asks quote-grounded questions over RAG excerpts; every example-bearing subquestion is paired with a no-example version and a counter-perspective barriers question; outputs contain three to five summary/quote bullets and are later sorted by an LLM judge.
evidence_records.Fine-tuning or adaptation: No weight fine-tuning reported; adaptation uses task decomposition, few-shot prompting, researcher-defined subquestions, RAG over text-embedding-3-large/Qdrant, temperature 0.0, empirically chosen similarity thresholds, and structured post-processing.
evidence_records.Single-agent or multi-agent: modular non-agent pipeline using different models for distinct steps; not an autonomous multi-agent architecture
evidence_records.Agent roles: No agents are defined. ChatGPT-4o performs thematic organization, RAG-based quote-grounded coding, and relevance sorting; o1 performs Task 1 cross-site synthesis; text-embedding-3-large and Qdrant retrieve excerpts.
evidence_records.Human role: Qualitative researchers define goals and output formats, manually perform small samples, author site summaries and code/subquestion frameworks, compare manual with assisted outputs, revise themes, validate and contextualize quotes, revisit transcripts, interpret results, and retain responsibility for final syntheses and intervention decisions; computer scientists implement secure task-specific pipelines.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: Task 1 site-level summary bullet within a care-practice domain; Task 2 retrieved transcript excerpt and quote-grounded bullet within a practice-area code, subquestion, and FQHC site
evidence_records.Generated outputs: Task 1 thematic groupings and draft cross-site syntheses for 22 domains; Task 2 a 19-code by 12-site matrix whose cells contain about 30 summary-statement/supporting-quote bullets, plus source-interview identifiers
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Task 1 instructs the model not to alter original bullet points and retains a miscellaneous category. Task 2 requires an illustrative quotation for every statement, records the source interview, returns retrieved excerpts, removes duplicate quotes, and uses a Python script to verify that every quoted string occurs in the transcripts; researchers revisit original transcripts for context.
evidence_records.Baselines: Manual no-LLM performance of the same tasks: two researchers cross over manual versus assisted synthesis for two comparable Task 1 domains; Task 2 compares the assisted method with manual coding of six interviews from two sites across four codes of different complexity. Multiple candidate model families were explored during workflow development.
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: Task 1 small-scale comparison covers two researchers and two domains; Task 2 small-scale comparison covers six interviews, two sites, and four codes. Repeated stochastic runs, random seeds, and per-configuration run counts are not reported.
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: No automatic metric is used to establish qualitative interpretive quality. The workflow uses embedding similarity thresholds (initially 0.4, lowered to 0.3), exact quotation validation/deduplication, and descriptive time comparisons; the authors explicitly reject agreement/overlap as sufficient gold-standard measures for these tasks.
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: Task 1 uses a two-researcher crossed comparison: each researcher manually synthesizes one of two similar domains and uses LLM outputs for the other, then compares quality and timing. Task 2 compares manual with assisted analysis on six interviews from two sites and four codes, followed by research-team assessment against task-specific rigor and utility criteria; blinding and independent external evaluation are not reported.
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: Task 1 explicitly includes two qualitative researchers. Task 2 includes at least one qualitative researcher and team discussion, but the exact evaluator count and individual expertise are not fully enumerated; the collaboration spans qualitative, health-services, clinical, and computer-science expertise.
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: not reported; the authors argue that inter-rater reliability or thematic overlap cannot by itself capture interpretive depth and use expected variation between competent human researchers as a practical benchmark
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: No inferential test, confidence interval, or formal uncertainty analysis is reported; evaluation is qualitative and descriptive, with per-researcher time reductions and projected coding-time calculations.
evidence_records.Principal results: For Task 1, LLM organization was comparable to human grouping, but model syntheses lacked actionable nuance, novelty judgment, and contextual correction; researchers retained interpretive control. Assisted synthesis reduced time by 30% for one researcher and 55% for the other. For Task 2, model and human findings were often complementary, but RAG fragmentation caused tangential retrieval, loss of perspective, and overgeneralization; quote/source access let researchers validate and contextualize outputs. The scaled workflow integrated 167 interviews across 19 practice areas into intervention refinements that the team judged infeasible on the deadline by manual coding alone.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: Task 1 time fell by 30% and 55% for the two researchers in the small comparison. Manual Task 2 coding took 20 hours for three transcripts across four codes; the authors project approximately 310 hours for one site and 93 full-time workweeks for all 12 sites at that observed pace. Monetary cost is not reported; ChatGPT-4o was chosen over o1 for Task 2 based on cost and efficiency.
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: Advarra IRB approval (Pro00071432) and informed consent are reported. High-risk medical data were processed through Stanford SecureGPT; commercial/open tools were rejected when security, institutional approval, scale, cost, or opacity were unsuitable. Data remain restricted for confidentiality, and the discussion addresses bias, decontextualization, reflexivity, transparency, and loss of researcher familiarity.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: The paper reports the task framework, models, temperature, retrieval thresholds, output structure, and workflow diagrams; supplementary sections are cited for domains, code definitions, prompts, subquestions, and interface details. Code is publicly identified as github.com/sronaghi/LLMsinQualAnalysis. Data are restricted, and dated model snapshots, random seeds, complete run logs, and the cited supplement were not present in the inspected 20-page PDF.
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: LLM outputs can lack nuance, novelty judgment, perspective, and context; RAG can fragment data and surface tangential excerpts; models may overfit examples and favor positive accounts; large-team/site variation changes model behavior; researchers may lose data familiarity if reading is delegated; existing commercial/open tools can be insecure, expensive, opaque, inflexible, or unable to handle the corpus; and current models lack long-context/domain reasoning needed for direct insight generation.
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: The small-scale comparisons cover only two Task 1 domains and six Task 2 interviews/four codes, use participating researchers rather than blinded independent evaluators, and report no formal uncertainty or repeated-run stability. Task-specific sufficiency was determined by the same interdisciplinary team developing the workflow. Efficiency projections extrapolate one observed manual rate, and proprietary model snapshots are not dated.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Extends task-specific human–AI collaboration principles and prior human-versus-LLM qualitative coding/theme studies by embedding secure LLM workflows in a real, large multi-site applied-health study. It uses LLooM/CollabCoder and earlier evaluation work as methodological context but contributes distinct iPATH workflows and outcomes.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Direct evidence for human-centered task decomposition, plurality-aware evaluation, quote/source provenance, context-loss diagnostics, secure sensitive-data processing, workflow-specific efficiency measurement, and why agreement/overlap metrics cannot substitute for interpretive quality in large-scale qualitative analysis.

quality_dimensions: Strength and independence of its baselines
Availability of data, prompts, code, and model versions
Whether conclusions are proportionate to the evidence

quality_scores.Title: Large Language Models for Large-Scale, Rigorous Qualitative Analysis in Applied Health Services Research

Clarity of its qualitative methodology.rationale: Adequate: the paper distinguishes comparative-case-study context, qualitative synthesis, and deductive coding and ties evaluation to explicit task-specific criteria of qualitative rigor.

Appropriateness of its dataset.rationale: Adequate: two authentic analytic tasks use a large, heterogeneous, sensitive 12-site health-services corpus whose scale and applied deadline directly motivate the framework's claims.

Transparency of its computational workfl.rationale: Adequate: models, task decomposition, RAG, thresholds, temperature, prompts' functional content, quotation validation, post-processing, and human decision points are described.

Strength and independence of its baselin.rationale: Partial: manual performance of the same tasks and several candidate models provide relevant comparators, but the manual samples are small and the developing research team also evaluates the assisted workflow.

Adequacy of its human evaluation.rationale: Partial: qualitative researchers compare manual and assisted outputs against task-specific rigor/utility criteria, but evaluator counts are incomplete for Task 2 and there is no blinding or independent external assessment.

Validity of its automatic metrics.rationale: Absent for qualitative quality: no automatic metric is used or validated as a measure of interpretive quality; similarity thresholds and exact quote checks support retrieval/provenance only.

Treatment of interpretive plurality.rationale: Adequate: the design explicitly rejects a single gold standard, treats expected differences between competent researchers as a benchmark, and reports complementary human/model perspectives rather than collapsing them to agreement.

Evidence grounding and traceability.rationale: Adequate: every Task 2 statement requires a transcript quotation and source identifier, quotations are programmatically verified, retrieved excerpts remain visible, and researchers revisit transcripts for context.

Stability and reproducibility testing.rationale: Partial: the framework is tested across researchers, domains, sites, codes, and candidate models, but repeated stochastic runs, seeds, and quantitative stability estimates are not reported.

Ethics, privacy, and responsible-researc.rationale: Adequate: IRB approval, informed consent, restricted-data rationale, secure institutional model access, tool-security screening, human control, bias, context loss, and reflexivity risks are substantively addressed.

Availability of data, prompts, code, and.rationale: Partial: a public code repository and cited prompt/subquestion supplements support reuse, but confidential data, dated model snapshots, seeds, run logs, and the cited supplement are absent from the inspected PDF.

Whether conclusions are proportionate to.rationale: Partial: the paper reports concrete workflow limitations and preserves a central human role, but broad claims that the framework preserves rigor rest on one study and small, non-independent comparison samples without formal uncertainty.

quality_scores.Interpretation caution: The total is a compact audit aid, not a ranking of study quality; dimensions must be interpreted individually against the paper's stated claim.
